title: Ibrahim at the House
hook: make this city safe, and make me and my offspring keep up prayer (14:35–41)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the good word and the good tree, roots firm and branches in the sky. Your line was a good word is a tree. Who got your good word, and what did you say? Day four hundred forty-seven.

You met Hajar in the valley many months ago, near the start of this path: a mother, a baby, a water skin, and a man walking away who said God had commanded it. Surah Ibrahim goes back to that valley from the other side: the father's. It keeps his prayer, line by line. A long report in Bukhari has him saying part of it as he walked away from them that day; the prayer also thanks God for two sons given in old age, so commentators differ over when each line was said. Either way, we overhear a father's whole list of requests.

Listen to what he asks for, in order. First: my Lord, make this city safe. Not rich, not famous. Safe. Then: keep me and my sons from worshiping idols; they have led many people astray. Then, in verse thirty-seven, in paraphrase: our Lord, I have settled some of my children in a valley with no crops, by Your sacred House, so that they may keep up the prayer. So make the hearts of people yearn toward them, and provide them with fruits, so that they may be grateful. Notice he doesn't ask for fruit first. He asks for hearts. People's hearts, turning toward a valley with no crops. Then he thanks God for giving him Isma'il and Ishaq in his old age. And then the line in Pickthall's translation: "My Lord! Make me to establish proper worship, and some of my posterity (also); our Lord! and accept the prayer." Make me keep up the prayer, and some of my children after me. And last: our Lord, forgive me, and my parents, and the believers, on the day the reckoning is set up. Some Muslims recite those last two verses near the end of their own prayer, just before the closing greetings. So a father's words at the House come back inside the prayer of people who face that same valley. He asked that his children would keep the prayer, and his words are said in it.
screen: `MAKE THIS CITY SAFE.` · `MAKE HEARTS YEARN TOWARD THEM.` · `MAKE ME KEEP UP THE PRAYER.` · `FORGIVE ME AND MY PARENTS.` · then, large: `MAKE US KEEP THE PRAYER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for your children, or future ones. Sit, and breathe. Bring to mind the children in your life: your own, or ones you hope for, or nieces, nephews, students, the kids next door. Picture their faces. What would you ask for them, if you made a list like Ibrahim's? Safety? Good hearts around them? A practice that holds them? If you pray, you can recite Ibrahim's words, or ask in your own language. If not, simply hold them in mind with care. The bell holds the time.
Ibrahim at the House. The old father's prayer in Surah Ibrahim: a safe city, hearts that yearn, and children who keep up the prayer. Today's word.
Your line: make us keep the prayer. Today, write your own short list of what you hope for the children in your life, and keep it somewhere safe. Day four hundred forty-seven.

howItsDone: Some Muslims recite Ibrahim's words from 14:40–41, rabbi j'alni muqima s-salati, in the final sitting of the daily prayer before the closing salam, and parents often say them for their children.

fork.setup: you're Ibrahim, old, at the House in a valley with no crops. you can ask God for one thing first. what does he ask?
fork.reveal: make this city safe. then: keep us from idols, make hearts yearn toward them, and make me and my children keep up the prayer.

original.note: Arabic: "my Lord, make me one who keeps up the prayer" (14:40).

trapdoor: what you thought: an old man praying for his family.
what it means: a father asking for safety, open hearts and faithful prayer for his children, words some still say in their own prayer.
what a scholar hears: 14:35–41 is a single extended du'a; scholars note 14:41 asks forgiveness for his parents, read alongside 9:114 on Ibrahim's father.

sources.quoted: My Lord! Make me to establish proper worship, and some of my posterity (also); our Lord! and accept the prayer.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 3364 (Hajar and the infant in the valley; Ibrahim's prayer as he leaves)

notes: Pickthall wording of 14:40 quoted from memory; please confirm exactly.
Recitation of 14:40–41 in the final tashahhud is a common practice, not a requirement; confirm the wording 'many Muslims'.
'Thousands of years ago by tradition's reckoning': no date given; confirm.
The trapdoor's note on 14:41 and 9:114 (forgiveness for his parents) touches a known exegetical discussion; confirm it's fair.
Year 1 day 39 told Hajar's story; this day refers back to it and focuses on Ibrahim's prayer.

Editor review (y2 444–462): the hook stated as fact that the prayer came years later with Isma'il grown and the House built; Bukhari 3364 has Ibrahim saying 14:37 as he left Hajar and the infant, so the hook now says commentators differ on timing. Cut unsourced 'millions travel there every year', 'one of the few places in the Qur'an', 'thousands of years ago', 'five times a day' and the narrator's 'every prayer since has been part of the answer'; 'my children' corrected to 'some of my children' to match 14:40; 'many Muslims' softened to 'some'.
